{"id": "53:39/q11", "question": "What continuing benefit do cited reports describe?", "turns_on": "Which report and kind of continuing credit is cited.", "positions": [{"id": "53:39/q11/p1", "position": "After death, three sources continue: charity, beneficial teaching or practice, and a righteous child's prayer.", "reasons": "A Prophetic report is cited by al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr and Study Quran; Imam al-Ṣādiq names guided practice. Ibn Kathīr treats these as effects of one's own work, citing 36:12."}, {"id": "53:39/q11/p2", "position": "A sick believer still receives credit for habitual deeds performed while healthy.", "reasons": "Imam al-Ṣādiq reports the Prophet's account of God's instruction to the recording angel during illness."}, {"id": "53:39/q11/p3", "position": "The Prophet recited these verses, said the return-to-God formula, and became subdued.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports the practice."}]}
{"id": "53:39/q12", "question": "Can worship or gifts be performed for the deceased?", "turns_on": "Whether the act discharges a duty, gifts reward, or is bodily or financial.", "positions": [{"id": "53:39/q12/p1", "position": "Proxy devotional acts are barred unless specific evidence permits them.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī's school and al-Ṭabrisī name Hajj as an exception. Al-Qurṭubī reports agreement that no one prays for another. Ibn ʿĀshūr says an act cannot discharge another's personal duty, while assuming financial liability for accidental killing is prescribed support."}, {"id": "53:39/q12/p2", "position": "Bodily acts differ from financial acts, and gifting reward is prayer for grace.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports the bodily/financial distinction; Ibn al-Humām attributes one to Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī. Al-Khafājī locates dispute in discharge of another's bodily duty during or after life, with or without permission; feeding and asking God to convey reward are different."}, {"id": "53:39/q12/p3", "position": "Both bodily and financial good can benefit the deceased.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya invokes Saʿd's charity for his mother; al-Qurṭubī reports ʿĀʾisha's retreat and manumission for her brother and the Prophet's permission of charity, water being best. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī separates gifting reward from proxy performance."}, {"id": "53:39/q12/p4", "position": "An heir's proxy fasting belonged to early Islam and was abrogated.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭaḥāwī preserves proxy Hajj but not fasting."}]}
{"id": "53:39/q13", "question": "May pilgrimage be performed for another?", "turns_on": "Whether Hajj is delegable and what conditions apply.", "positions": [{"id": "53:39/q13/p1", "position": "Proxy Hajj is allowed for a dead or unable person under varying conditions.", "reasons": "The Prophet authorizes it for a deceased father and likens a dead sister's vow to paying God's debt. Al-Shāfiʿī permits it; the Ḥanafīs require incapacity lasting to death, with recovery requiring personal Hajj; Aḥmad does not. Ibn Ḥabīb permits a son without bequest and an elderly person's proxy; Ibn al-Qaṣṣār allows it for dead but not incapacitated living persons; Ibn ʿArafa bought it for a ruler under a non-Mālikī school."}, {"id": "53:39/q13/p2", "position": "Mālik generally rejects it, except when a will stipulates it.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿĀshūr report the limitation. Ibn al-Faras counts bequeathed obligatory Hajj as the deceased's striving; al-Bājī says Mālik enforced a bequest and required the hired proxy to have done Hajj first."}, {"id": "53:39/q13/p3", "position": "Some authorities dislike or forbid proxy Hajj.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jallāb dislikes hiring for an incapable person but does not void the agreement. Some Mālikī books report a different Abū Ḥanīfa position; one Shāfiʿī opinion forbids it citing this verse."}, {"id": "53:39/q13/p4", "position": "The Prophet affirmed a child's Hajj and the mother's separate reward.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī and Bursevī transmit the question and answer."}]}
{"id": "53:39/q14", "question": "Does gifted Qur'an recitation or voluntary worship reach the dead?", "turns_on": "Whether recitation is transferable and how intention or payment affects it.", "positions": [{"id": "53:39/q14/p1", "position": "Recitation's reward does not reach the deceased.", "reasons": "Al-Shāfiʿī and followers cite the verse, absence of Prophetic recommendation or Companion precedent, and the rule that worship requires text rather than analogy. Al-Nawawī calls it the well-known Shāfiʿī view; the Itqān author's school agrees. Another Shāfiʿī view excludes voluntary prayer and other voluntary acts."}, {"id": "53:39/q14/p2", "position": "Recitation and voluntary rewards can reach the deceased.", "reasons": "The other three imams, Aḥmad and some Shāfiʿīs are reported in favor; Ibn al-Faras reports Mālik's school permits it and Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects an unsupported blanket ban attributed to Mālik. Al-Biqāʿī includes recitation among beneficial ties. Ibn ʿĀshūr compares ʿĀʾisha's protective recitation over the Prophet and cites payment for al-Fātiḥa as healing."}, {"id": "53:39/q14/p3", "position": "Ask God after recitation to convey its reward; paid recitation apparently yields none.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī favors supplication after reciting, though some require initial intention. Payment for teaching is lawful. Ibn ʿĀshūr says hired Hajj is possible through its expense, but prayer and fasting apparently cannot be hired."}]}
{"id": "53:39/q15", "question": "How is striving understood on the spiritual path?", "turns_on": "Whether the spiritual fruit is earned, divinely granted, or beyond ordinary striving.", "positions": [{"id": "53:39/q15/p1", "position": "Effort belongs to wayfaring; realization depends on divine carrying or attraction.", "reasons": "Al-Naṣrābādhī contrasts the paths of wayfaring and Reality, seeing the kingdom and seeing the King, with poems about the rare traveler and the beloved. Bursevī cites Jāmī: years of exertion cannot arrive without divine attraction. He says effort and attraction meet in God and many paths converge."}, {"id": "53:39/q15/p2", "position": "Striving, its visibility, recompense, annihilation, and renewed life mark successive stations.", "reasons": "Al-Warrāq maps vv. 39–43 to beginner, middle, end, loss of individual will, and second arising. Bursevī adds witnessing, subsistence, bodily nourishment and delayed lawful provision."}, {"id": "53:39/q15/p3", "position": "Pure deeds earn Paradise, while vision and nearness are gifts to the spirit.", "reasons": "Al-Baqlī says deeds must lack ostentation; Paradise levels are earned, but unveiling, witness and intimacy come by God's grace."}, {"id": "53:39/q15/p4", "position": "Reward and punishment follow settled dispositions; spiritual returns differ.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says repeated acts shape dispositions, though divine decree governs immediate fortunes; he names bodily resurrection, return to primordial heart and return to gifted Real existence after annihilation, only the first universal."}, {"id": "53:39/q15/p5", "position": "Self-knowledge and restraint of desire safeguard effort.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā al-Hāshimī says most striving follows desires."}]}
{"id": "53:39/q16", "question": "What rhetorical principles do the cited notes invoke?", "turns_on": "Whether rhetorical force comes from contextual syntax or studied literary arrangement.", "positions": [{"id": "53:39/q16/p1", "position": "Meaning and arrangement, learned through poetry and grammar, ground rhetorical merit.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says poetry, advanced grammar and taste allow one to understand Qur'anic inimitability; rhetorical causes should be investigated. Al-Jāḥiẓ warns against claiming nothing remains to learn. Tamīm, ʿAdī, Bashshār and al-Buḥturī liken verse making to intellectual craft and measured arrangement, not pleasant sounds or ease of letters. A group dismisses poetry and advanced grammar; al-Jurjānī condemns that stance."}, {"id": "53:39/q16/p2", "position": "Context decides whether near-negation means near failure or no approach to occurrence.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says 2:71's mā kādū yafʿalū implies eventual action, unlike the poem's lam yarahā wa-lam yakad; the conditional idhā gives past lam yakad future force."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q01", "question": "What does سعيه mean?", "turns_on": "Whether striving names outward work or its inward intention.", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q01/p1", "position": "A person's work, deeds, or effort.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba gloss saʿy as work or deed. Bursevī links the sense to 92:4, where efforts differ, and says these teachings are in the scrolls."}, {"id": "53:40/q01/p2", "position": "A person's intention.", "reasons": "Al-Warrāq cites the report that people are raised according to their intentions."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q02", "question": "How does سعيه clarify the preceding ما in 53:39?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q02/p1", "position": "It supports reading ما as a verbal noun denoting the work accomplished.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers this reading; a verbal noun can denote its object, just as خلق الله can mean God's created thing."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q03", "question": "How is وأن سعيه connected with the preceding scriptural statements?", "turns_on": "Whether the coordination keeps verse 40 inside the earlier scriptures or introduces a further statement.", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q03/p1", "position": "It coordinates with the earlier أن and remains among the teachings in the scriptures.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya traces the coordination to the understood أن in verse 38; he says the majority read fatḥa while Abū al-Sammāl reads kasra from verse 42 onward. Al-Samīn allows genitive, nominative, or accusative case for both وأن clauses. Ibn ʿĀshūr says emphatic أن fits this consequence of a person's possessing only his own effort."}, {"id": "53:40/q03/p2", "position": "It begins Qur'anic commentary on the earlier scriptural statement rather than remaining within it.", "rea
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

sons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr alternatively coordinates it with relative ما under the preposition bi in verses 36–37: the people were not told this truth. Islāhī says extensions grounded in the original statement begin at verse 40 and turn the discourse toward Quraysh."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q04", "question": "Does أن require an omitted pronoun of شأن here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q04/p1", "position": "No; سعيه itself serves as the noun of أن.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says this also removes any need to reduce أن."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q05", "question": "What time does سوف mark?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q05/p1", "position": "It marks a future event, usually understood as distant.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives the usual force of سوف. Elmalılı says the effort's fruit need not appear immediately, yet the effort is not lost."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q06", "question": "How is يُرى read and grammatically construed?", "turns_on": "Whether an active verb can take an implied object pronoun without leaving أن improperly construed.", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q06/p1", "position": "The passive reading means that effort is shown or seen.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Baghawī derive it from 'I showed him the thing'; al-Ālūsī also gives that derivation. Al-Samīn prefers visual perception on the passive because interpreting it as knowing needs an omitted second object. Al-Zajjāj allows an active construction but prefers this reading."}, {"id": "53:40/q06/p2", "position": "An active reading is permissible with an implied object pronoun referring to effort.", "reasons": "Abū Isḥāq, al-Khalīl, Sībawayh and associates, Muḥammad ibn Yazīd, and al-Zajjāj permit it as سوف يراه. Al-Mubarrid says أن necessitates the omitted pronoun because the clause would otherwise have two governors; the Basran analogy is إن زيدا ضربت. Al-Samīn says only أن governs سعيه, while يرى governs the pronoun, so this is not double government by تنازع or اشتغال; he rejects calling the pronoun far-fetched."}, {"id": "53:40/q06/p3", "position": "The active reading is forbidden or weak.", "reasons": "The Kufans say أن and يرى would both govern سعيه. Abū al-Baqāʾ calls the active fatḥ reading anomalous and weak because it leaves the noun of أن without a predicate. Al-Zajjāj calls analogous إن زيدا سوف أكرم weak unless a pronoun is supplied or the construction changed to إن زيدا سأكرم. Al-Samīn disputes the alleged double government and the objection to an implied pronoun."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q07", "question": "What does it mean that effort will be seen?", "turns_on": "Whether seeing denotes direct presentation of deeds, knowledge of them, their recompense, or a visible embodiment.", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q07/p1", "position": "The deeds or effort themselves will be displayed and witnessed at the Resurrection.", "reasons": "Muqātil says worldly deeds appear in the Hereafter. Al-Zajjāj says God already knows them, but the servant sees them on his balance. Al-Naḥḥās and al-Wāḥidī include good and bad deeds; al-Baghawī and al-Nasafī specify the scale. Al-Burṣawī, al-Ālūsī, and Elmalılı add the record. Rāzī says disclosure brings joy to believers and grief to unbelievers. Ibn Kathīr compares 9:105; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ cites 3:30 and 99:6–8 for deeds made present."}, {"id": "53:40/q07/p2", "position": "The person's effort will be made known or understood.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba glosses 'will be seen' as 'will be known'; al-Wāḥidī and Ibn al-Jawzī transmit him. Asad says God makes people understand their life deeds. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes seeing as a metaphor for certain, widespread public knowledge and compares 7:49."}, {"id": "53:40/q07/p3", "position": "What is seen is the effort's recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī transmits this as a second view of Judgment Day; al-Qurṭubī says God shows a person the recompense. Al-Ṭabrisī explains seeing the deeds as being repaid for them. Rāzī calls a figurative reading in which one sees the reward of service before a king remote: verse 41 separately promises full recompense."}, {"id": "53:40/q07/p4", "position": "A past deed may itself return in a visible, even beautiful, form.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports a righteous deed shown in beautiful form and argues that every existent can be seen and God can restore what ceased to exist. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows embodied visible deeds or identification by signs, citing 18:49, the believers' light in 66:8, and a banner assigned to each traitor."}, {"id": "53:40/q07/p5", "position": "God may be the one who sees the effort.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites 9:105 for this alternative."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q08", "question": "By whom will the striving be seen?", "turns_on": "Whether the passive points chiefly to the doer, other witnesses, or intentionally leaves the observer open.", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q08/p1", "position": "The person who performed it will see it.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj places it in the servant's balance; al-Wāḥidī, al-Nasafī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, Elmalılı, Asad, and Study Quran likewise emphasize the person's sight or understanding. Al-Ṭabrisī says the servant sees and receives full repayment."}, {"id": "53:40/q08/p2", "position": "God and other witnesses, as well as or besides the performer, will see it.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya names God and those present; Rāzī allows God as viewer and compares 9:105. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says the passive suggests someone besides the performer. Study Quran links 9:105, where God, the Messenger, and believers see deeds."}, {"id": "53:40/q08/p3", "position": "The passive leaves the viewer unspecified.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says being seen itself brings pleasure or shame regardless of who sees it."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q09", "question": "How are efforts displayed or identified at reckoning?", "turns_on": "Whether the display is through scales, written records, visible forms or signs, or public disclosure.", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q09/p1", "position": "They are visible on the balance.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī reporting al-Zajjāj, al-Nasafī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, and Elmalılı locate the deeds on the scales."}, {"id": "53:40/q09/p2", "position": "They are seen written in the person's record.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports this view; Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, and Elmalılı mention record and scale together."}, {"id": "53:40/q09/p3", "position": "They may appear as embodied deeds or as identifying signs.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports righteous deeds in beautiful form and says God can restore what has ceased. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 18:49 and 66:8, the light going ahead of believers, and the Prophetic report of a banner for every traitor."}, {"id": "53:40/q09/p4", "position": "Their truth may be established through public knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the exchange in 7:49 and calls seeing a metaphor for certain, widespread knowledge."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q10", "question": "Why is the viewer left unnamed by the passive verb?", "turns_on": "Whether the passive chiefly universalizes the effect of exposure or points to additional observers.", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q10/p1", "position": "The fact of being seen itself produces joy or shame whoever sees.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī explicitly links the unspecified viewer to pleasure for good effort and shame for evil effort."}, {"id": "53:40/q10/p2", "position": "The passive implies an observer besides the person who performed the deed.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ draws this inference from the passive form."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q11", "question": "What is the effect of showing people's deeds?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q11/p1", "position": "It honors and gladdens the good, and rebukes, grieves, or shames wrongdoers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says public presentation honors good people and rebukes wrongdoers; Rāzī says believers rejoice, perhaps before everyone, while unbelievers grieve. Al-Biqāʿī says being seen itself gives pleasure or shame. Al-Ālūsī calls it glad tidings and rebuke. Ibn ʿĀshūr speaks of good reputation or public disgrace."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q12", "question": "How does seeing effort relate to its full recompense in the next verse?", "turns_on": "Whether 'seen' already means reward or precedes the distinct recompense of verse 41.", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q12/p1", "position": "Display comes first; full repayment follows.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Bayḍāwī, and al-Ṭabrisī make the sequence explicit. Al-Naḥḥās, Ibn Kathīr, Islāhī, Kur'an Yolu, and Study Quran couple presentation with just recompense. Al-Ṭabrisī takes the following pronoun as referring to effort: the effort itself is repaid, with lasting reward for obedience. Rāzī says the next verse's separate mention of repayment argues against taking seeing as reward."}, {"id": "53:40/q12/p2", "position": "Seeing can itself mean receiving the recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports that what appears on Judgment Day is reward; al-Qurṭubī says God shows the person's recompense. Rāzī rejects this as remote because verse 41 separately addresses recompense."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q13", "question": "What is the referent and syntax of the repayment pronoun in verse 41?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q13/p1", "position": "It refers back to effort, which is repaid in full.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī assigns the pronoun to effort. Rāzī reports a parsing in which جزى takes two objects, or three with a preposition that can be omitted; he cites 76:12."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q14", "question": "Why and how may the fullest reward be delayed?", "turns_on": "Whether the future wording points to postponed completion of recompense or an added supreme reward.", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q14/p1", "position": "Full reward comes later, although reward can start at death.", "reasons": "Rāzī says 'then' may indicate delay in recompense or simply advance the discourse. He answers the concern about a righteous person's wait: reward starts at death and reaches completion in Paradise. Elmalılı like

wise says effort's fruit need not be immediate and will not be lost."}, {"id": "53:40/q14/p2", "position": "The 'most complete' reward may be an added reward beyond Paradise: seeing God.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers this reading because an unrestricted superlative calls for what exceeds every otherwise complete reward; he compares 10:26."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q15", "question": "What does this promise teach about deeds and accountability?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis is comprehensive judgment or the worth of honest personal effort.", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q15/p1", "position": "Every good and bad deed is accounted for and justly repaid, however small.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says both kinds of deeds are seen and repaid; Ibn Kathīr specifies good for good and evil for evil. Islāhī says even tiny good deeds count and no small evil is ignored; Kur'an Yolu says every freely chosen deed is brought forward and judged with complete justice. Study Quran says deeds testify to a person's life."}, {"id": "53:40/q15/p2", "position": "Honest effort and earning by one's own labor have value before God.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu draws this teaching from the verses."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q16", "question": "How do the neighboring statements address the fears and hopes of righteous people and sinners?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q16/p1", "position": "The wording leaves sinners hope of forgiveness and reassures the righteous about what they earn.", "reasons": "Rāzī says bearing no other's burden does not exclude God's forgiving one's own burden. For the righteous, 'only what he strives for' affirms receipt of what is earned; phrasing it as 'not what he did not strive for' would not. This balance expresses mercy preceding wrath."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q17", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from a person seeing their striving?", "turns_on": "Whether seeing effort exposes dependence on grace, removes self-credit, or discloses stages of the inward path.", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q17/p1", "position": "One sees one's striving is unfit for God and survives only through divine grace.", "reasons": "Tustarī and Sahl say the servant learns what the striving merits; without the Lord's grace, it would perish or cause the servant to perish."}, {"id": "53:40/q17/p2", "position": "Striving is not a means of earning reward.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī says this of the Prophet's striving in al-Sulamī, and Bursevī reports the principle without that limitation."}, {"id": "53:40/q17/p3", "position": "Recognition of a work's defects makes one dislike credit for it.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥafṣ says one disowns attribution of deficient work to oneself and dislikes being recalled for it."}, {"id": "53:40/q17/p4", "position": "The path of striving moves through beginning, middle, and end, with distinct gifts at the end.", "reasons": "Al-Warrāq says annihilation is rewarded with witnessing and subsistence with bodily nurture, including lawful provisions deferred on the path."}, {"id": "53:40/q17/p5", "position": "Striving has four inward levels, each with its own result.", "reasons": "Bursevī describes the ego's purification from violations and natural conformity, yielding gardens; the heart's removal of darkness and veils, yielding abandonment of worldly desire, pleasure, adornment, wealth, and rank; the secret's polishing through divine attributes, yielding their manifestations; and the spirit's essential theophanies, yielding extinction of ego and subsistence in oneness."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q18", "question": "What report illustrates the public exposure of wrongdoing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q18/p1", "position": "God will expose before creation one who publicizes something his brother dislikes.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn ʿĀshūr both transmit the Prophetic report; it illustrates the disgrace of a public display."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q19", "question": "What report supplies a visible sign of betrayal at Judgment Day?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q19/p1", "position": "A banner will be raised for each traitor, identifying the betrayal.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the Prophetic hadith as an example of efforts identified by signs."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q20", "question": "What is reported of the Prophet when he recited these verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q20/p1", "position": "He recited the istirjāʿ formula and became subdued.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits this from Ibn ʿAbbās."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q21", "question": "What incident is reported as the setting for this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q21/p1", "position": "A report links it to ʿUthmān stopping his donations after his foster brother promised to bear his sins.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports this from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, al-Kalbī, and other exegetes. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Sarḥ received a camel; the account says ʿUthmān left his post at Uḥud, then resumed his former practice."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q22", "question": "How does this passage fit the sūra's movement toward earlier scripture?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q22/p1", "position": "The passage turns from reflection on creation to enduring teachings in the scriptures of Moses and Abraham.", "reasons": "Study Quran describes the third section's transition and its perennial truths. Islāhī says reliance on descent from those prophets for Paradise is condemned and attention goes to their teachings and sacrifices."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q23", "question": "What do the cited literary examples show about figurative images?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q23/p1", "position": "A single image can support several different comparisons.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says a sparking flint can suggest generosity, sharp intelligence, success, or reaching an aim; failure to spark can suggest miserliness, dullness, or fruitless effort. The moon can suggest fame, distinction, honor, elevation, completion, and decline. He cites Abū Tammām's growing noble child, al-Buḥturī's rising honor, an unnamed poet's life cycle, Ibn Bābak's vizier's partial royal authority after Fakhr al-Dawla appointed Abū ʿAlī, and Abū Bakr al-Khwārizmī's wealthy versus poor host."}]}
{"id": "53:40/q24", "question": "What determines whether a word sounds apt in a literary context?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:40/q24/p1", "position": "A word's merit comes from its fit with neighboring words, not from its isolated sound or meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says أخدع works in al-Ḥamāsa and al-Buḥturī but burdens a line by Abū Tammām; شيء works in ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa and Abū Ḥayya but weakens al-Mutanabbī's line about the revolving heavens. If merit inhered in a word alone, its effect would not change between settings."}]}

{"id": "53:42/q05", "question": "What does the definite article in al-muntaha specify?", "turns_on": "Al-Razi ties the article's reference to whether 'your' addresses people generally or the Prophet.", "positions": [{"id": "53:42/q05/p1", "position": "For a general addressee it identifies the already promised return.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says revelation and the Prophet have previously announced this return."}, {"id": "53:42/q05/p2", "position": "For the Prophet as addressee it is generic, encompassing every terminus.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says every terminus goes to the Lord who is its origin; in the corresponding account perception starts from outward things and through reflection reaches God and stops."}]}
{"id": "53:42/q06", "question": "What ultimately ends with the Lord?", "turns_on": "The notes dispute whether the unrestricted 'ending' denotes bodily return, final outcomes, hopes, the limit of thought, causal explanation, or all kinds of ending; al-Tabatabai argues against restricting its scope.", "positions": [{"id": "53:42/q06/p1", "position": "Creatures return to God after death or at resurrection for judgment and recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas, al-Thaʿlabi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, and others add recompense for good and bad deeds; al-Wahidi calls this the exegetes' interpretation. Ibn ʿAtiyya calls it the gathering and destination after death, relative to worldly life. Al-Razi calls resurrection the well-known interpretation and says it answers when the prior recompense occurs: gratitude is rewarded and ingratitude punished. Al-Kashshaf cites 35:18; al-Nasafi cites 3:28. Ibn Kathir specifies Judgment Day, Study Quran says all then stand before God, and al-Alusi says no other being has an independent or shared part in their return. Al-Bursevi cites 42:53 and says beginning and end are in God. Al-Biqai includes bodily resurrection and the return of deeds; Elmalili includes full recompense and calls God First and Last. Islahi says no one can evade accountability by appealing to another and God's decisions are final. Kuranyolu says judgment gives full recompense without the slightest injustice, while grace and forgiveness remain God's choice and believers should hope without complacency. Al-Tabatabai rejects making this the only meaning as too narrow."}, {"id": "53:42/q06/p2", "position": "The ultimate destination is specifically God's reckoning, reward in Paradise, or punishment in Hell, where earthly action ends.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya contrasts Paradise or Hell as the absolute endpoint with the postmortem gathering relative to worldly life, and posits an omitted genitive: the end of God's mercy or punishment. Al-Tabrisi names divine reward and punishment where deeds cease; Ibn Kathir reports Muʿadh ibn Jabal saying the return ends in Paradise or Fire. Al-Alusi reports reckonings, Paradise, and Fire as commentators' glosses. Study Quran cites 13:35 for the Garden of the reverent versus the Fire of disbelievers. Al-Tabatabai rejects restriction to reward and punishment or reckoning as unsupported narrowing."}, {"id": "53:42/q06/p3", "position": "All beneficence begins with God and all hopes, or security, finally end with Him.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabi and al-Baghawi report beneficence and hopes; al-Qurtubi has favor and security. Al-Jishumi lists grace and hopes among reported senses."}, {"id": "53:42/q06/p4", "position": "Human inquiry and thought reach their limit at God, whose essence and attributes cannot be encompassed.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi permits reasoning about created things but says divine knowledge, essence, and modality elude comprehension. Al-Jishumi reports the limit of thought; al-Alusi applies it to divine essence and attributes. Reports from Ubayy, Anas, Abu Hurayra, Ibn Abbas, and Abu Dharr support stopping or turning to creation, detailed in the reflection question. Al-Razi interprets Ubayy's and Anas's reports as reaching the uncaused necessary existent; he says reflection from outward objects stops at God. Al-Tabatabai rejects making the limit of thought the verse's only sense, while treating the Imam al-Sadiq's instruction as an expanded application of 'ending.'"}, {"id": "53:42/q06/p5", "position": "All beings, their effects, governance, deeds, knowledge, hopes, and every other ending depend on God, their origin as well as final end.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabai reads the unrestricted infinitive noun absolutely: God creates beings and their relations, directly or through causes, and all governance returns to Him; he cites 39:62–63 and 7:54. Al-Biqai includes bodily return and deeds, knowledge, hopes, affairs, place, and time. Asad includes the universe's beginning and end in time and space, God as source and goal. Bursevi cites 42:53 for affairs returning to God because there is no other deity. Al-Husayn's explanation of tawhid, transmitted by al-Sulami and Bursevi, says contingent effects arise from God, return to Him, and vanish while their cause remains; al-Sulami cites 'He is the First' in 57:3. Al-Razi reads the generic article as every terminus belonging to its origin."}, {"id": "53:42/q06/p6", "position": "The chain of causes and rational inquiry ends at God as the uncaused Necessary Being and source of existence.", "reasons": "Al-Razi argues contingent things require causes and an explanatory chain cannot finish with another contingent thing. {"id": "53:42/q07", "question": "What guidance about contemplating God is drawn from the verse and its reports?", "turns_on": "Whether the transmitted prohibitions express the verse's whole sense or an application directed especially to those unready for difficult inquiry.", "positions": [{"id": "53:42/q07/p1", "position": "Stop speculation about God Himself and reflect on His creation instead.", "reasons": "Ubayy ibn Kaʿb's Prophetic report is transmitted by al-Thaʿlabi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir, al-Biqai, al-Durr, and al-Alusi; some explicitly give no grading. Anas or Sufyan al-Thawri transmit 'when the Lord is mentioned, stop.' Abu Hurayra, Ibn Abbas, and Abu Dharr transmit the creation-versus-Creator instruction because thought cannot encompass Him, with Abu Dharr warning of ruin. Al-Thaʿlabi's Abu Hurayra report describes layers of earth, heavens, and a sea in the seventh heaven. Ibn Kathir says the wording of Abu Hurayra's raised report is not preserved; he cites a sound Satanic-question hadith requiring refuge and stopping, and a Sunan report including an angel's three-hundred-year earlobe-to-shoulder distance. Al-Qurtubi also links the Satanic-question hadith and cites a poem directing thought from God's essence to His works. Al-Durr transmits Yunus ibn Maysara's account of the companions discussing God's greatness and the Prophet redirecting them, and a Kufa imam's report of reflection on the sun and a radiant western land inhabited by beings unaware whether Adam or Iblis was created. Al-Biqai adds Ibn Abbas's inability-to-grasp-God's-measure report. Imam al-Sadiq applies the verse to stopping speech when it reaches God. Imam al-Baqir warns Ziyad that forbidden disputation brings doubt, void deeds, and confusion, or wandering in a variant. Al-Wahidi specifies that divine knowledge, essence, and modality cannot be comprehended; al-Alusi says most transmitted proofs indicate the essence cannot be known in its full reality. Al-Jishumi gives no grading for the creation report."}, {"id": "53:42/q07/p2", "position": "The warning especially guides people unprepared for difficult rational inquiry; the stop-at-God report is an expanded application of 'ending.'", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabai says difficult speculation risks lasting ruin for such people, and interprets Imam al-Sadiq's instruction as a broader application rather than limiting the verse's entire meaning.
